Package index

Tables from an ARD — reading the ARD

The recommended start: an analysis results dataset (cards / cardx) made ready for a table. Acts on: an ARD data frame. normalize_ard() flattens it – groups and hierarchy become ordinary key columns – and widen_ard() does the whole ARD half in one call, giving a table data frame now. list_ard_keys(), pull_ard(), overall_row() and cell_rows() look inside an ARD and shape its rows. Start with the Get started article.

ard-tables
Tables from a cards/cardx ARD

Flatten an ARD into an explicitly keyed long table
widen_ard()
Turn a normalized ARD into a wide table data.frame
list_ard_keys()
What is actually inside an ARD
pull_ard()
Pull a statistic out of an ARD, keyed like the spread columns
overall_row()
Where the table's overall row comes from
cell_rows()
Several rows in one cell recipe, each with its own fallback chain

Tables from an ARD — the plan

table_plan() names the roles (what goes across, what goes down) and each plan_*() verb adds one declaration – cells, labels, levels, stub, blank rows, pages, widths, header, titles. Nothing runs until the plan is handed to rtf_tables() or plan_apply(), which give rtftable pages; a later layer wins over an earlier one. The header and the denominators in it agree with the columns by construction. The Excel definition of a table lives in tflspec, which builds a plan from it (tflspec::tfl_table_plan()).

Document, rendering & tokens

rtf_document() creates the document – with the program, the program_fallback and tokens of your own (tokens =) for its headers and footers; the section and content calls below add to it; generate_rtfreport() writes the file. Acts on: the rtf_document object. rtf_page() and rtf_default_format() are the only settings that are document-only – everything else in this reference acts on a table. rtf_config() edits an already-composed document; rtf_document() starts a new one. rtf_text_tokens() lists every {TOKEN} a header, footer, title or footnote can carry ({PAGE}, {PROGRAM}, {PROGRAM_FULL}, {DATETIME}, your own).

Configure document-level settings

Build a page watermark

Generate an RTF file from a report object

Sections — headers & footers

A section applies a running header / footer to a range of pages. Acts on: the rtf_document object. Headers and footers are themselves small tables: build their rows with rtf_header() / rtf_footer() (a list of rows – to change one, make it again).

rtf_section()
Define sections for pages
rtf_header() rtf_footer()
Create a header or footer object for a section

Page content — tables, titles & footnotes

Place a table on the page, with its titles and footnotes. Acts on: the rtf_document object – rtf_tables() takes the rtftable objects the sections below produce. Note the two levels: rtftable() sets how a table looks; passing the same setting to rtf_tables() overrides it for that placement only, leaving the table object untouched.

Assign content titles to pages
rtf_footnotes()

Print an rtftable object
format(<rtftable>)
Render an rtftable body as console text
summary(<rtftable>)
Summarise an rtftable object

Package defaults

Inspect and reset the rtfreporter.* option defaults (paper size, orientation, margins, font, font size). Acts on: nothing – these set the fallbacks every other function uses when you do not pass a value. A site can set its own in Rprofile.site; see the page-setup article.

rtfreporter_options()

rtfreporter_reset_defaults()

Bring your own table — as_rtftables()

The second path: a table already built elsewhere – a gt::gt() table, a gtsummary table, an rtables/tern VTableTree, a tfrmt, flextable or huxtable table, an rlistings listing_df, or a plain data.frame – turned into rtftable objects, reading the source’s metadata and paginating in one call. Acts on: the source object. Produces: rtftable objects. as_rtftables() returns one per page (a list); as_rtftable() returns a single object. stub_cols() prepares a tidy data.frame beforehand by merging hierarchy columns into one indented stub column; stub_spec() carries the same settings into as_rtftables(stub = ).

as_rtftables()
Convert a table object into rtfreporter table pages
as_rtftable()
Convert one table object to a single rtftable
combine_sections()
Combine table page lists into one auto-sectioned list
stub_cols()
Merge hierarchy columns into one indented stub column
stub_spec()
Bundle the row-stub settings for as_rtftables()

Recipes — four complete tables from data frames

Copy-and-run examples for the four table shapes a clinical report is mostly made of: demographics, adverse events, PK concentrations and a laboratory shift table. Each runs end to end, data in and RTF out, and they are shown together because their arguments barely overlap – what a demographics table needs, an adverse-events table does not.

rtfreporter-recipes
Four complete recipes: DM, AE, PK and LB

Column headers

Build and edit the column-header block. Acts on: an rtftable – there is no header setting at document level. col_cell() describes one header cell and is accepted by rtf_col_header(), rtftable(col_header = ) and rtf_tables(col_header = ). A whole header built with rtf_col_header() goes to the same places plus set_col_header(). Coordinates are those of the finished table, so a merged stub counts as one column. col_key() lets a cell name the columns it covers by a column-name segment instead of by position.

col_cell()
Column-header cell specification
col_key()
Select header columns by a column-name segment
rtf_col_header()
Build a multi-row column-header specification
set_col_header()
Set the whole column header of a finished table (final-table coordinates)
header_map()
Show the column header of every page, cell by cell
rtf_columns()
Column names of a finished table's body
rtf_header_source()
Deparse a table's column header back to editable rtf_col_header() source

Post-hoc styling verbs

Restyle a table you have already built, without rebuilding it. Acts on: an rtftable, or a list of them – every verb here has a list method, so one call styles every page. These are the last word: they override whatever rtftable() or the source adapter set. set_decimal_split() is the exception in kind – it does not change the data, only how a numeric column is rendered.

style_header() style_cols() style_body() style_zone() add_header_row()
Restyle an existing rtftable (post-hoc styling verbs)
collapse_repeats()
Blank out consecutive repeated values in a finished table
set_decimal_split()
Line up the decimal points of a numeric column

Built-in cell-format functions

Re-shape the TEXT of cells so counts and percentages line up. Acts on: a data.frame or a character vector, before it becomes a table. Pass one to rtftable(cell_format = ) / as_rtftables(cell_format = ) to apply it during the build instead.

fmt_value_paren()

fmt_right_align()

Numeric display formatters & rounding

Turn numbers into the strings a clinical table prints – significant digits, rounding, alignment. Acts on: a data.frame or a numeric vector, before it becomes a table. Numbers reaching rtftable() unformatted are converted with as.character(), which is rarely what a report wants, so format first. round_num() is the rounding rule every formatter (and a plan’s templates) uses – R’s half-to-even, or SAS’s half-away-from-zero with options(rtfreporter.rounding = "sas").

fmt_signif()
Format numbers to a number of significant digits
fmt_round()
Format numbers to a fixed number of decimal places
fmt_numeric()
Format the numeric columns of a table for display
round_num()
Round the way R rounds, or the way SAS rounds

Pagination strategies & helpers

Split a table across pages. Acts on: the body of a table being built. Vertical splitting is chosen with as_rtftables(split = ) – a strategy name ("group_safe", "group_force", "by_value", "rows", "none") with its settings given as ordinary arguments alongside it, or a function of your own for a bespoke rule. paginate_cols() is the horizontal counterpart: it acts on a FINISHED rtftable, splitting a too-wide table by column and repeating the row headings on every page.

paginate_cols()
Paginate a table horizontally, by columns
add_cont_label()
Prepend a continuation label row to a paginated chunk

Column-width utilities

Measure text and size columns to their content. Acts on: a data.frame; returns widths in twips for rtftable(column_widths_twips = ). Use auto_col_widths() when long labels wrap; as_rtftables(auto_width = TRUE) does the same during the build, clamped to the writable page width.

text_width_in()
Estimate the display width of a text string
auto_col_widths()
Automatically calculate column widths for a data.frame

Listings (source data → listing body)

Reshape source data into what a listing prints, before any of it is rendered: source variables joined into one printed column, a long cell wrapped over several physical rows, narrow gutter columns, and a blank row after each record. Acts on: a data.frame / tibble. Produces: a data.frame, which as_rtftables() renders. listing_col() describes one printed column and listing_spec() the listing as a whole; build_listing() applies the spec, and as_rtftables(listing = ) runs the same work inside the pipeline and derives the header, the widths and the alignment from it. An rlistings listing_df needs none of this – it is already laid out, and goes straight to as_rtftables(). fit_listing_widths() proposes every column’s width from the page and the data, and listing_code() prints the spec as source to paste and tune. listing_wrap() is the rule that breaks a cell into lines, and listing_wrap_code() writes that rule out as source when a listing needs a different one – calling listing_disp_width(), listing_take() and listing_split_after(), the measurements a rule is built on, rather than copying them. catx() is the join a listing column makes, exported for the columns you build yourself.

listing_col()
One printed column of a listing
listing_spec()
Bundle the settings for one listing
build_listing()
Reshape a data.frame into a listing body
fit_listing_widths()
Propose the listing's column widths from the page and the data
listing_code()
Print a listing spec as the code that would build it
listing_wrap()
Break a listing cell or header into the lines it occupies
listing_wrap_code()
The default wrapping rule, as source to edit
listing_disp_width() listing_take() listing_split_after()
The measurements a listing's wrapping rule is built on
catx()
Join values with a separator, skipping the missing ones

Figures

Place a plot or an image file on a page. rtfplot() wraps a PNG / JPEG (or a plot object, saved for you); rtf_figures() adds figures to the document, with titles and footnotes, as rtf_tables() does for tables. Acts on: the rtf_document object.

rtfplot()

print(<rtfplot>)
Print an rtfplot object

Assembling a deliverable & post-processing

Join finished RTF FILES into one, with a table of contents and continuous page numbering. Acts on: files on disk, not R objects – this is the step after generate_rtfreport(). The table of contents is a table (file, label, heading, level) – assemble_folder() makes it from a folder – or the path of one (.xlsx / .csv). rtf_replace_text() edits a rendered file in place – text a report needs only at delivery time.

assemble_rtf()
Assemble multiple RTF files into one
assemble_folder()
Assemble every RTF in a folder into one TOC deliverable
rtf_replace_text()
Replace text inside a generated RTF file

Borders

Two constructors, and only two: rtf_border_line() describes one edge – its line style, width and colour – and rtf_border() collects edges into the border of a cell, a row or a zone, including the rules inside a selection (inside_h, inside_v). Where usable: both are accepted by rtftable(border = ), rtf_tables(border = ) and the style_*() verbs; rtf_border() is also accepted by col_cell(border = ). There is no border setting at document level. Later wins, per edge – a style_*() call overrides rtftable(), which overrides the adapter. The constructors these two replaced are listed under Deprecated at the bottom of this page; ?rtf_border pairs the old and the new spelling for every case.

rtf_border_line() rtf_border_side()
Single-edge border specification
rtf_border() rtf_border_none() rtf_border_top() rtf_border_bottom() rtf_border_box()
Four-edge border specification for a cell or row

Shared table styles (S3, snapshot)

One object carrying borders, alignment, padding and row height, so a set of tables can share a look. Where usable: rtftable(style = ) and rtf_tables(style = ). rtf_table_style_with() derives a variant from an existing style, changing only the fields you name.

Working with an AI assistant

The package is too new to be in a chat model’s training data, so an assistant has to be told the API before it writes any. Two briefings ship inside the package for that – one for using rtfreporter, one for working on it – and this returns the copy installed alongside your version, which is the one that matches what you actually have.

rtfreporter_ai_manual()
The AI assistant manuals that ship with this package

Deprecated – scheduled for removal

The border constructors that rtf_border_line() and rtf_border() replaced at 0.5.0 / 0.6.0. They still work and each warns once per session, naming its replacement, and are removed in 0.9.0, the first CRAN release – do not write new code against them. ?rtf_border pairs the old and the new spelling for every case. rtf_border_none(), rtf_border_top(), rtf_border_bottom() and rtf_border_box() are documented on the rtf_border() page itself. Deprecated in 0.8.x by the pre-CRAN API review, and removed in 0.9.0 too: rtf_border_side() (now rtf_border_line(), documented on its page), the header editors below (write the header in rtf_col_header() / rtf_header() instead), paginate() (use as_rtftables()), and the arguments rtftable(spanning_header = ) and as_rtftable(gt_obj = ) (now x), the as_rtftables() arguments stub_vars / stub_label / stub_indent / stub_group_summary (now stub =), and the assembly helpers below (assemble_folder() and assemble_rtf(toc = <a table>)).
